title: Severe epigastric pain going through to the back in a 56-year-old builder
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 56-year-old builder in the ED. He woke with severe epigastric pain going through to his back after a night of heavy drinking. The candidate then interprets his observations, bloods and venous gas, ECG and abdominal ultrasound report. They give the diagnosis and differentials, outline management in the emergency department, answer his worry about cancer and set escalation triggers.
focus: Acute epigastric pain radiating to the back: diagnosing alcohol-related acute pancreatitis, finding its cause and grading its severity, and starting early management
stem: You are an intern in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital, just before lunchtime. Your next patient is Gary Pearson, a 56-year-old builder who has come in with severe abdominal pain. He has been triaged, has an IV cannula in and has had bloods sent. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Gary and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his observations, his blood results and venous gas, his ECG and an abdominal ultrasound report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting, and answer the examiner's questions (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Gary Pearson, a 56-year-old builder. You are sitting up on the trolley, leaning forward and hugging your tummy. You are sweaty and in a lot of pain. You don't want to move, because moving makes the pain worse. You are a down-to-earth bloke and you talk openly about your drinking once you are asked. You are not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "Mate, I've got this terrible pain in my guts. I couldn't even go to work."

The pain (give only when asked)

  • Site: right in the middle of your upper tummy, between the ribs and the belly button.
  • Onset: it woke you at about 5 am and has slowly got worse since then. You have never had pain like this before.
  • Character: sharp and stabbing.
  • Radiation: it goes straight through to your back.
  • Better or worse: leaning forward helps a bit. Moving hurts. Nothing else has helped.
  • Severity: 9 out of 10.
  • It is constant. It does not come and go in waves, and it is not a tearing or ripping pain.

Associated symptoms (only when asked)

  • Nausea and vomiting: you vomited twice last night and once at about 3 am, all before the pain woke you at 5 am. It was food and drink. There was no blood and nothing like coffee grounds.
  • Your appetite is gone.
  • Bowels: normal yesterday. You are passing wind. No diarrhoea, no black stools, no blood.
  • Systemic: no fever or shivers, no weight loss, no night sweats.

Negatives (only if asked about each)

  • No crampy pain after fatty food before this. No yellow skin or eyes, no pale stools, no dark urine.
  • No heartburn or indigestion before this. No anti-inflammatories (ibuprofen, Nurofen) and no aspirin. No vomiting blood.
  • No chest pain, no tightness, no breathlessness, no palpitations. No cough.
  • You have not collapsed or fainted.
  • No pain or burning when you pass urine and no blood in it. No loin pain.
  • No injury to your tummy. No recent travel and nobody sick around you.

Past history, medicines and allergies

  • High blood pressure. The last reading at your GP was 140/90.
  • High cholesterol. You are not on a tablet for it; your GP told you to fix your diet.
  • No operations.
  • Amlodipine 5 mg once a day. No other medicines, no supplements, no steroids.
  • Marijuana occasionally with mates, about one joint every few months since your teens. No other drugs.
  • No known allergies.

Family history

  • Your mother had a heart attack at 80.
  • Your father got type 2 diabetes at 65.

Social history

  • Smoking: half a pack a day since you were 18.
  • Alcohol: 4 beers (full-strength stubbies) a night, more on weekends. Last night you had about 12 beers at a mate's party, vomited, and you feel "hungover". Your last drink was at about 1 am.
  • If asked the CAGE questions:
    • Cut down: "Yeah, I've thought about cutting back."
    • Annoyed: "Yeah, a bit. It's how I socialise with my mates."
    • Guilty: no.
    • Eye-opener: no, you never drink in the morning.
  • You have never had the shakes, a fit or seen things when you stopped drinking, and you have never been treated for withdrawal.
  • Work: a builder. You are active at work but do no other exercise.
  • Diet: pies and sausage rolls for lunch, takeaway for dinner.
  • Home and support: you live with your girlfriend of 5 years. You have plenty of friends and family.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Idea: "Bad hangover? Maybe from all the vomiting?"
  • Concern: you are worried it might be cancer. You also couldn't go to work today.
  • Expectation: something for the pain, and to know what is going on.

The nurse and how Gary changes

  • If the candidate asks for observations, the nurse gives the triage set: RR 19, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 130/85, HR 109 regular, temperature 37.3 °C, alert, pain 9/10, BGL 6.2 mmol/L. Height 177 cm, weight 100 kg (BMI 32).
  • Partway through the history, the nurse says: "He's just vomited again, about 100 mL of yellow-green fluid, no blood."
  • If the candidate orders IV analgesia, the nurse gives it. A few minutes later Gary says the pain is about 6/10 and he talks more easily, but he still won't lie flat. If no analgesia is given, he stays at 9/10.
  • If the candidate orders an antiemetic, fluids or anything else, the nurse confirms she will arrange it, and the examiner says: "Noted. Please cover your management in Part 2."
  • If the candidate asks for an ECG, blood results or imaging, the examiner says they will be given in Part 2.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: obese man, sitting forward, sweaty and in obvious pain. Smells faintly of alcohol. Alert and oriented.
  • Hydration: dry mucous membranes. CRT 2 seconds, warm peripheries.
  • Hands, eyes and skin: no jaundice. No palmar erythema, spider naevi, gynaecomastia or other stigmata of chronic liver disease. No tremor and no asterixis.
  • Abdomen, inspection: obese, not obviously distended, moves a little with breathing. No scars. No bruising around the umbilicus or in the flanks.
  • Abdomen, palpation: marked tenderness in the epigastrium, with voluntary guarding and milder tenderness in the left upper quadrant. No rigidity and no rebound tenderness. Murphy's sign negative. No palpable organs. No pulsatile or expansile mass, although his size makes this hard to feel.
  • Percussion and auscultation: no shifting dullness. Bowel sounds present but reduced.
  • Renal angles: not tender. Hernial orifices: normal.
  • Pulses and BP: femoral and foot pulses present and equal. BP 130/85 right arm, 128/84 left arm.
  • Chest: equal expansion, resonant to percussion, clear breath sounds including both bases. No surgical emphysema in the neck or chest wall. Heart: dual heart sounds, no murmurs.
  • Rectal examination: if offered, the examiner says it is not needed.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self, confirms Gary's identity and gains consent before examining.
Acknowledges his severe pain with empathy and asks the nurse for IV analgesia early (ideally with an antiemetic), without waiting until the whole history is finished.
Asks about alcohol in a non-judgemental way and uses plain language throughout.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: epigastric (between the ribs and the umbilicus), going straight through to the back
Onset and course: woke him at 5 am, gradually worse since, constant, never had it before
Modifying factors: better leaning forward, worse on moving

check.x: Characterises the vomiting: twice last night and once at about 3 am, food and drink; asks specifically about blood or coffee grounds (none) and when the vomiting started relative to the pain (all the vomiting came before the pain woke him at 5 am; pain after forceful vomiting raises Boerhaave syndrome, and blood after retching would suggest a Mallory-Weiss tear).
Screens for a biliary cause: previous colicky pain after fatty food, jaundice, pale stools and dark urine (all absent).
Screens for the life-threatening mimics: chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations (ACS) and tearing pain or collapse (ruptured AAA).
Screens for the other differentials:

kids.x: Peptic ulcer or perforation: NSAIDs or aspirin, previous indigestion, haematemesis, melaena
Bowel obstruction and gastroenteritis: bowels opening, passing wind, diarrhoea, sick contacts
Pneumonia and pyelonephritis: cough, urinary symptoms, loin pain
Systemic symptoms: fever, weight loss, night sweats

check.x: Takes a quantified alcohol history:

kids.x: Usual intake and binge: 4 beers a night (about 5 to 6 standard drinks), more on weekends, about 12 beers last night
Time of last drink (about 1 am) and past withdrawal (no shakes, fits or hallucinations, no eye-opener)
A dependence screen such as CAGE (2 of 4: has thought about cutting down, annoyed)
kids.d: Credit AUDIT-C or another validated screen instead of CAGE.

check.x: Takes the past history, medications and allergies: hypertension (last 140/90) on amlodipine 5 mg daily, hypercholesterolaemia, no operations, no NSAIDs or steroids, occasional marijuana, no known allergies.

Takes the family and social history: mother MI at 80, father T2DM at 65; half a pack a day since 18 (about 19 pack-years); builder, no other exercise; pies and takeaway; lives with his girlfriend of 5 years, good support.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is a bad hangover from vomiting, worried it is cancer, missed work.
Examination
Asks for the full set of vital signs and assesses hydration: HR 109, dry mucous membranes, CRT and peripheral perfusion.
General inspection: sweaty, in pain, sitting forward, obese; checks for jaundice, stigmata of chronic liver disease and tremor (none).
Inspects the abdomen, including for periumbilical or flank bruising (Cullen and Grey Turner signs, absent).
Palpates gently, starting away from the pain: epigastric tenderness with voluntary guarding, no rigidity or rebound (no peritonitis), Murphy's sign negative.
Feels for a pulsatile, expansile mass and checks the femoral and distal pulses (and credits BP in both arms).
Auscultates the bowel sounds (reduced), and examines the chest including the bases (effusion, pneumonia), the heart and the renal angles.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: all values are in the white zone, but HR 109 rising to 114 with ongoing vomiting and no urine output means volume depletion. If no analgesia has been given (pain still 9/10), recognises that uncontrolled pain meets the SAGO additional criteria for a clinical review; if analgesia was given (6/10), notes partial response and the need for ongoing titration.
States that typical pain plus a lipase of 1850 U/L (more than 3 times the upper limit) meets the diagnostic criteria (2 of 3 needed; the ultrasound makes it all 3).
check.d: Credit, but do not require: the enzyme level does not reflect severity.

check.x: Interprets the raised WCC and haematocrit as inflammation and haemoconcentration, with SIRS (HR >90, WCC >12) as a marker of risk of severe disease.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: CRP 50 as a marker of inflammation, and that a CRP above 150 mg/L at 48 hours predicts severe disease.

check.x: Uses the bloods to find the cause and look for organ failure: isolated raised GGT with normal ALT/bilirubin (fits alcohol), normal calcium and triglycerides (2.6 mmol/L, not causative), and normal creatinine, SpO2 and BP (no renal, respiratory or cardiovascular failure).
Interprets the ECG as sinus tachycardia with no ST or T wave changes: no evidence of an inferior MI presenting as upper abdominal pain.

Interprets the ultrasound: no gallstones and a CBD of 4 mm (biliary cause unlikely, no ERCP needed); bulky hypoechoic pancreas with peripancreatic fluid (pancreatitis); normal-calibre aorta (AAA excluded).
check.d: Credit, but do not require: fatty liver.

check.x: Gives acute alcohol-related pancreatitis as the most likely diagnosis, currently without organ failure (severity cannot be graded until 48 hours; he has risk markers for severe disease). Justifies it with at least 3 of: heavy drinking with a binge last night, epigastric pain through to the back eased by leaning forward, lipase more than 3 times the upper limit, ultrasound changes with no gallstones, and an isolated raised GGT.
check.d: Credit naming the revised Atlanta classification (mild, moderately severe, severe) but do not require it.

check.x: Gives at least 3 differentials, each with a feature for or against it from this case, including at least one of: perforated peptic ulcer (no rigidity, no NSAIDs), ruptured AAA (normal aorta, normal BP) or ACS (no chest pain, normal ECG). Others: gallstone pancreatitis (no stones, normal ALT), Boerhaave syndrome (no chest pain, no surgical emphysema, lipase markedly raised), gastritis or Mallory-Weiss tear (no blood, lipase markedly raised).
Management
Starts goal-directed IV crystalloid (e.g. Hartmann's) with reassessment, avoiding aggressive large volumes, and sets a urine output target (≥0.5 mL/kg/h, about 50 mL/h) with a fluid balance chart.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: an ABCDE approach, two large-bore cannulae and an IDC.

check.x: Gives titrated IV opioid analgesia (e.g. morphine or fentanyl in small increments) with an antiemetic (e.g. ondansetron), and avoids NSAIDs.
check.d: Credit regular paracetamol (IV or oral) as part of multimodal analgesia.

check.x: Allows early oral intake as tolerated instead of prolonged nil by mouth, with enteral (nasogastric) feeding if he cannot eat; does not give prophylactic antibiotics.
check.d: Credit nil by mouth for now while he is vomiting, if early feeding is planned as soon as it is tolerated.

check.x: Gives parenteral thiamine before glucose and starts alcohol withdrawal monitoring with symptom-triggered benzodiazepine.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: the dose (e.g. 300 mg IV daily), naming an alcohol withdrawal scale, diazepam on senior advice, and noting the last drink at 1 am.

check.x: Gives at least 1 supportive step: VTE prophylaxis (enoxaparin 40 mg subcut daily), monitoring and correcting electrolytes, calcium and glucose, nicotine replacement therapy.
Admits him under surgery or gastroenterology with a senior informed, reassesses severity over 48 hours, and arranges HDU or ICU review if organ failure develops.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: CT is not needed now; it is for diagnostic doubt or deterioration.

check.x: Safety netting

Explains to Gary in plain words that his pancreas is inflamed, most likely from alcohol, and that it is not a hangover. Answers the cancer worry honestly: cancer is very unlikely because the scan and the story point to alcohol-related inflammation, and further imaging would follow if it does not settle as expected. Checks his understanding.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: prognosis (most recover within a week; watched closely for 2 days).

check.x: Advises that it can come back if he keeps drinking, recommends stopping alcohol completely, and arranges follow-up: at least 1 of drug and alcohol team referral, smoking cessation support, GP review after discharge.

Asks the nurses for at least hourly observations and to escalate at least 3 of: rising HR, falling BP, rising RR or falling SpO2, urine output below target, fever, worsening pain, confusion, or tremor, sweating or hallucinations (withdrawal). Asks for a clinical review for any yellow-zone value and a rapid response for any red-zone value.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: telling Gary to call the nurse at once for worse pain, breathlessness, the shakes or vomiting blood.

part2.lead: Here are Gary's observations, his blood results and venous gas, his ECG and the abdominal ultrasound report.
part2.patient:
Question 4 opens with Gary's question. React to the answer:

  • If the candidate explains clearly that cancer is very unlikely and why, look relieved: "Thank Christ for that."
  • When alcohol is raised, ask: "Do I have to give up completely? It's how I catch up with my mates." Accept it if the candidate explains kindly and offers support. If you are lectured, go quiet.
  • If the candidate uses jargon (pancreatitis, lipase, Atlanta), ask: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: On room air. Triage set at 11:20 and the nurse's repeat set at 12:20. No urine passed since arrival.
handover.model:
• Examiner note: the 12:20 pain score is blank. If the candidate ordered analgesia in Part 1, tell them it is 6/10 and IV analgesia has been given. If not, tell them it is 9/10 and no analgesia has been given.
  • Read: at 11:20, RR 19, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 130/85, HR 109 and temperature 37.3 °C are all in the white zone, with pain 9/10. At 12:20, HR has risen to 114 (still white), temperature 37.6 °C and BP 126/80 (white). He has vomited again and has not passed urine.
  • Meaning: a persistent and rising tachycardia, with vomiting and no urine output, means volume depletion from vomiting and third-space losses around the inflamed pancreas. HR above 90 is one SIRS criterion. There is no respiratory or circulatory failure now. If no analgesia has been given (pain still 9/10), uncontrolled pain meets the SAGO additional criteria for a clinical review; if analgesia was given (6/10), there is a partial response and analgesia needs ongoing titration.
  • Changes: a clinical review now (this review), analgesia, goal-directed fluids, hourly observations with a fluid balance chart, a clinical review for any yellow-zone value and a rapid response for any red-zone value.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: severe epigastric pain, vomiting. IV cannula, bloods sent
Vomited about 100 mL bilious fluid, no blood. No urine passed. Pain score: see examiner

handover.label: Bloods and venous blood gas
handover.result: Collected 11:30 at cannulation; venous gas on room air at the same time. Sample not haemolysed. No previous results on file.
handover.model:
• Read: lipase 1850 U/L (more than 30 times the upper limit) and amylase 920 U/L. WCC 14.8 with neutrophils 12.1, CRP 50, haematocrit 0.52. GGT 245 with normal bilirubin, ALP, ALT and AST. Calcium, magnesium, phosphate, UEC, glucose 6.2 and albumin are normal. Triglycerides are 2.6 (non-fasting). The venous gas is normal, with a lactate of 1.5.
  • Meaning: typical pain plus lipase more than 3 times the upper limit confirms acute pancreatitis; the height of the lipase does not grade severity. A raised WCC with HR above 90 meets SIRS criteria, and the raised haematocrit shows haemoconcentration; both mark a risk of severe disease. A raised GGT alone fits heavy alcohol use. A normal ALT and bilirubin make a gallstone cause less likely. Normal calcium and triglycerides far below the level that causes pancreatitis exclude those causes. Normal creatinine, with normal SpO2 and BP, means no organ failure now, and the lactate is normal.
  • Changes: admit and give goal-directed fluids. Repeat UEC, haematocrit, calcium, glucose and CRP (CRP above 150 at 48 hours predicts severe disease). Treat the cause: alcohol.

labs.title: Liver function, pancreatic enzymes and lipids

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result: 12-lead ECG, 11:40. Sinus tachycardia, rate 108/min, regular. Normal axis. PR 160 ms. QRS 90 ms. QTc 430 ms. No ST elevation or depression in any territory, including II, III and aVF. No T wave inversion. No pathological Q waves. No previous ECG for comparison.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus tachycardia at 108/min with normal intervals and axis, and no ST or T wave changes or Q waves.
  • Meaning: the tachycardia fits pain and volume depletion. No evidence of an inferior MI, which can present as epigastric pain and vomiting in a man with his risk factors (smoker, hypertension, high cholesterol, obesity).
  • Changes: ACS is unlikely. The candidate may add a troponin if any doubt remains, and repeat the ECG if the pain changes in character.

handover.label: Abdominal ultrasound
handover.result:
Examination: ultrasound of the upper abdomen and aorta, 12:40.

Clinical details: 56-year-old man, severe epigastric pain radiating to the back since 5 am after heavy alcohol intake last night, vomiting. Lipase 1850 U/L. ?Pancreatitis ?Gallstones ?AAA.

Findings:

  • Pancreas: diffusely bulky and hypoechoic, with a thin rim of peripancreatic fluid and echogenic, oedematous peripancreatic fat around the body and tail. No discrete collection. No focal mass seen. Pancreatic duct not dilated. Views limited in part by body habitus and bowel gas.
  • Gallbladder: normal size, thin-walled. No gallstones or sludge. Sonographic Murphy sign negative. No pericholecystic fluid.
  • Bile ducts: common bile duct 4 mm. No intrahepatic duct dilatation.
  • Liver: normal size with diffusely increased echogenicity in keeping with fatty infiltration. Smooth surface. No focal lesion.
  • Spleen and vessels: spleen normal. Splenic and portal veins patent.
  • Aorta: normal calibre, maximum diameter 2.0 cm. No aneurysm.
  • Kidneys: normal size, no hydronephrosis.
  • Other: no free fluid elsewhere. No pleural effusion seen at either base.

Conclusion: sonographic features of acute pancreatitis. No gallstones and no biliary dilatation. Hepatic steatosis. Normal-calibre abdominal aorta.
handover.model:
• Read: a bulky, hypoechoic pancreas with peripancreatic fluid and fat oedema; no collection. No gallstones or sludge, CBD 4 mm. Fatty liver. Aorta 2.0 cm. No pleural effusion.
  • Meaning: confirms acute pancreatitis. No gallstones and a normal duct make a biliary cause unlikely, so with his drinking the cause is alcohol, and there is no indication for ERCP. The fatty liver fits alcohol and obesity. A normal aorta excludes AAA. No pleural effusion is reassuring for severity. Ultrasound does not show the whole pancreas well, but nothing here suggests a tumour.
  • Changes: treat as alcohol-related pancreatitis. CT is not needed now; contrast CT is kept for diagnostic doubt or for deterioration after about 72 hours, to look for necrosis or collections.

ask: You are now calling the general surgical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Gary Pearson, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Gary now, here in the emergency department.
Gary asks you, "Is it cancer, Doc, or did I just have a bad hangover?" Please answer him, then tell me what you would ask the nurses to watch for.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Gary Pearson, 56, builder.
  • Situation: acute pancreatitis, most likely alcohol-related, no organ failure at present; requesting admission.
  • Background: epigastric pain to the back since 5 am, 9/10, eased by leaning forward, vomiting four times; 12 beers last night, usually about 4 a night, last drink 1 am; hypertension on amlodipine, about 19 pack-years, BMI 32.
  • Assessment: HR 109 rising to 114, no urine passed, pain 9/10 untreated, or 6/10 after IV analgesia; lipase 1850; WCC 14.8, haematocrit 0.52, CRP 50; meets SIRS (HR >90, WCC 14.8); isolated GGT rise, normal ALT, bilirubin and calcium, triglycerides 2.6, not causative; normal creatinine, gas and lactate; ECG sinus tachycardia without ischaemia; ultrasound shows pancreatitis, no gallstones, CBD 4 mm, normal aorta.
  • Recommendation: I have started (or am starting) fluids, analgesia, an antiemetic and thiamine; please review for admission and severity reassessment.

Acute alcohol-related pancreatitis, currently without organ failure: heavy drinking with a binge, epigastric pain through to the back eased by leaning forward, lipase more than 30 times the upper limit, ultrasound changes, no gallstones, isolated raised GGT.

  • Gallstone pancreatitis: for: obesity, diet; against: no stones, CBD 4 mm, normal ALT and bilirubin.
  • Perforated peptic ulcer (must not miss): for: alcohol, smoking; against: no rigidity or rebound, no NSAIDs.
  • Ruptured AAA (must not miss): for: male smoker with hypertension, pain through to the back; against: normal BP, no mass, aorta 2.0 cm; partly, age 56, below the usual risk age.
  • Inferior MI: for: risk factors; against: no chest pain, ECG without ischaemia.
  • Boerhaave syndrome (must not miss): for: forceful vomiting after a binge before the pain began; against: no chest pain or breathlessness, no surgical emphysema, clear chest, no effusion, lipase markedly raised.

1. Resuscitate (ABCDE): two large-bore cannulae; goal-directed crystalloid (e.g. Hartmann's bolus, reassess, then titrated), avoiding aggressive large volumes; IDC or strict fluid balance chart, urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h or more.
  2. Titrated IV opioid, regular paracetamol and ondansetron; no NSAIDs.
  3. Early oral intake as tolerated, enteral if not; no prophylactic antibiotics.
  4. IV thiamine before glucose; alcohol withdrawal scale with symptom-triggered diazepam on senior advice.
  5. Enoxaparin 40 mg subcut daily; monitor electrolytes, calcium and glucose; nicotine replacement.
  6. Admit under general surgery; reassess severity over 48 hours (repeat CRP); HDU or ICU if organ failure; CT only for doubt or deterioration.

• Plain words: the pancreas, a gland behind the stomach, is inflamed, most likely from the alcohol; it is more than a hangover. The scan shows inflammation and no lump, and the drinking explains it, so cancer is very unlikely. If it doesn't settle as expected, we would do more scans. Most people recover within about a week, but we will watch you closely over the next 2 days because some cases become more serious.
  • Alcohol: it can come back if he keeps drinking. Stopping completely is the best protection. Offer the drug and alcohol team, smoking cessation support and GP follow-up after discharge. Check his understanding.
  • Nurses (at least hourly observations): rising HR, falling BP, rising RR or falling SpO2, low urine output, fever, worse pain, confusion, or shakes, sweats or seeing things; a clinical review for any yellow-zone value and a rapid response for any red-zone value.
  • Gary: call the nurse for worse pain, breathlessness or the shakes.

ddx.for: About 4 beers a night with 12 last night, constant epigastric pain through to the back eased by leaning forward, lipase 1850 U/L, a bulky pancreas with peripancreatic fluid on ultrasound, no gallstones and an isolated raised GGT.
He is obese and eats pies and takeaway, and gallstones are the commonest cause of pancreatitis.
ddx.against: No previous biliary colic, no jaundice, normal ALT and bilirubin, and no gallstones with a 4 mm bile duct on ultrasound.

ddx.for: Heavy alcohol use and smoking, with severe epigastric pain that is worse on moving.
ddx.against: No NSAIDs or previous indigestion, no rigidity or rebound, and the lipase is more than 30 times the upper limit.

ddx.dx: Ruptured or leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm
ddx.for: A male smoker with hypertension and pain going through to the back.
ddx.against: The pain is not tearing, BP is normal and equal in both arms, there is no pulsatile mass, the aorta measures 2.0 cm on ultrasound, and (partly) at 56 he is below the usual risk age.

ddx.for: He smokes and has hypertension, high cholesterol and obesity (his mother's MI at 80 is not a premature family history).
ddx.against: No chest pain or breathlessness, the pain is positional, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST or T wave changes.

ddx.for: Binge drinking with forceful vomiting before the onset of severe epigastric pain.
ddx.against: No chest pain or breathlessness, no surgical emphysema, clear chest, no pleural effusion on ultrasound, lipase more than 30 times the upper limit.

guide:
In Part 1, Gary answers the history and gives each detail only when asked. The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The nurse reports the further vomit partway through. If the candidate orders treatment in Part 1, say "Noted, please cover it in Part 2"; credit early analgesia under Professionalism. If they ask for an ECG, bloods or imaging, say these will come in Part 2.

In Part 2, hand over the observations, the bloods and gas, the ECG and the ultrasound report, then ask all four questions in order. The 12:20 pain score is blank. If analgesia was ordered in Part 1, tell the candidate it is 6/10 and IV analgesia has been given; otherwise tell them it is 9/10 and no analgesia has been given. Question 4 opens with Gary's own question.

Early oral feeding is current practice. Do not penalise a candidate who keeps him nil by mouth while he is vomiting, as long as they plan early feeding once it is tolerated. Do not credit prolonged fasting, prophylactic antibiotics or routine CT on arrival.

A high-performing candidate gets analgesia going early and characterises the pain, including its radiation to the back and the relief from leaning forward. They quantify the alcohol with the time of the last drink and screen for biliary disease, AAA and ACS. They examine the hydration, the abdomen for peritonism and an aortic mass, and the chest bases. In Part 2 they diagnose pancreatitis from the pain and a lipase more than 3 times the upper limit. They find the cause (no gallstones, isolated GGT, normal calcium and triglycerides) and check for organ failure. They give goal-directed fluids, analgesia, thiamine, withdrawal monitoring and early feeding, admit him, answer his cancer worry honestly and address his drinking without judgement.

A borderline candidate does not ask about the back, gallstones or alcohol quantity, reads the amylase and lipase only as "raised", or misses that the ultrasound excludes gallstones and AAA. They may forget thiamine and withdrawal, give antibiotics, or plan to discharge him.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute alcohol-related pancreatitis

Gary has constant, severe epigastric pain that goes through to his back, is eased by sitting forward and is worse on movement. He has vomiting and tachycardia, after a heavy binge on a background of daily drinking. Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when 2 of 3 criteria are met:

  • typical pain;
  • lipase (or amylase) more than 3 times the upper limit of normal;
  • characteristic imaging.

Gary meets all three. The height of the lipase confirms the diagnosis but does not tell you how severe the attack is. Lipase is preferred to amylase because it is more specific and stays raised for longer, so ordering both adds little.

Finding the cause: I GET SMASHED

The causes are:

  • Idiopathic
  • Gallstones
  • Ethanol
  • Trauma
  • Steroids
  • Mumps and other viruses
  • Autoimmune
  • Scorpion venom
  • Hypercalcaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia and hypothermia
  • ERCP
  • Drugs

Gallstones cause about half of cases, alcohol about a quarter, and 10 to 20% are idiopathic. Every patient needs an abdominal ultrasound for gallstones, plus calcium and triglycerides. An ALT above about 150 U/L early in the attack points to gallstones. Gary has no stones, a normal duct and a normal ALT, with a raised GGT alone, normal calcium and only mildly raised non-fasting triglycerides, so alcohol is the cause. A gallstone cause would change management: ERCP for cholangitis or a persisting duct stone, and cholecystectomy in the same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis.

Severity

The revised Atlanta classification grades severity:

  • Mild: no organ failure and no local or systemic complications.
  • Moderately severe: organ failure that resolves within 48 hours, or local complications such as collections or necrosis.
  • Severe: organ failure (respiratory, cardiovascular or renal) persisting beyond 48 hours.

Severity can only be confirmed after 48 hours, so early risk markers guide how closely to watch: SIRS (Gary has HR above 90 and WCC above 12), a raised haematocrit (haemoconcentration), rising urea or creatinine, age, obesity, a pleural effusion, and a CRP above 150 mg/L at 48 hours. Scores such as Glasgow-Imrie and BISAP may be used. Gary has no organ failure now: creatinine, SpO2 and BP are normal (no renal, respiratory or cardiovascular failure), and the lactate is normal.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: all white zone, but a rising tachycardia with vomiting and no urine output means volume depletion. Pain still 9/10 without analgesia meets the additional criteria for a clinical review; pain of 6/10 after analgesia is a partial response that needs ongoing titration.
  • Bloods: lipase confirms the diagnosis. WCC, CRP and haematocrit show inflammation and haemoconcentration. The LFT pattern, calcium and triglycerides point to the cause. Normal renal function, with normal SpO2 and BP, excludes organ failure for now, and the lactate is normal.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia without ischaemia; an inferior MI can present as epigastric pain and vomiting and must be considered in a man with his risk factors.
  • Ultrasound: confirms pancreatic inflammation, excludes gallstones and duct dilatation, and shows a normal aorta. Contrast CT is not routine at presentation. It is used when the diagnosis is uncertain, or when a patient fails to improve or deteriorates after about 72 hours, to look for necrosis and collections.

A well-prepared candidate would request: FBC, UEC, LFTs, lipase, calcium, magnesium and phosphate, glucose, triglycerides, CRP, a venous or arterial gas with lactate, an ECG, and an abdominal ultrasound. A group and hold, a troponin if ACS is a concern, and an erect chest X-ray or CT if perforation is suspected may be added.

Differentials that matter

  • Gallstone pancreatitis: the commonest cause overall, so it must be looked for.
  • Perforated peptic ulcer: sudden severe pain with peritonism and free gas. The lipase may rise modestly but rarely above 3 times the upper limit.
  • Ruptured or leaking AAA: back pain, collapse and a pulsatile mass in an older male smoker.
  • Inferior MI.
  • Boerhaave syndrome (oesophageal rupture): severe pain that follows forceful vomiting, classically after a binge, often with chest pain, breathlessness, surgical emphysema or a pleural effusion. Gary vomited before his pain began, so it must be considered; he has no chest pain or breathlessness, no surgical emphysema, a clear chest and no effusion, and his lipase is more than 30 times the upper limit.
  • Gastritis or Mallory-Weiss tear after a binge; a Mallory-Weiss tear shows as blood in the vomit after retching.

Bowel obstruction, hepatitis, pneumonia and pyelonephritis are screened for in the history.

Management

  • Resuscitation: ABC (ABCDE), two large-bore cannulae, and goal-directed IV crystalloid (Hartmann's is commonly used), titrated to HR, BP and a urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/h or more. Aggressive large-volume fluid gives no benefit and risks fluid overload.
  • Analgesia: titrated IV opioid with an antiemetic, with regular paracetamol (IV or oral) as part of multimodal analgesia; his LFTs are normal. Avoid NSAIDs while he is volume depleted.
  • Nutrition: current guidance favours early oral feeding as soon as it is tolerated rather than prolonged nil by mouth. Use enteral feeding (nasogastric or nasojejunal) if he cannot eat; it is preferred to parenteral nutrition.
  • No prophylactic antibiotics: they are kept for proven infection, such as infected necrosis or cholangitis.
  • VTE prophylaxis (enoxaparin 40 mg subcut daily). Monitor and correct electrolytes, calcium and glucose.
  • Treat the cause: alcohol cessation and thiamine for alcohol; ERCP for gallstones with cholangitis or a persisting duct stone; stop any causative drug; correct calcium or triglycerides.
  • Disposition: admit under general surgery or gastroenterology. Involve HDU or ICU for organ failure or a deteriorating patient.

Alcohol: withdrawal and Wernicke encephalopathy

Gary's last drink was at about 1 am, and withdrawal can begin within 6 to 24 hours. Give parenteral thiamine before glucose-containing fluids (for example 300 mg IV daily), as eTG recommends for hospitalised patients at risk, and monitor with an alcohol withdrawal scale. Treat withdrawal with symptom-triggered diazepam on senior advice. Tremor, sweating, agitation, hallucinations or confusion must be reported.

A CAGE score of 2 suggests problem drinking. Before discharge he needs:

  • a non-judgemental brief intervention, with advice to stop alcohol completely after pancreatitis (the NHMRC guidelines advise no more than 10 standard drinks a week and 4 on any day for healthy adults);
  • referral to drug and alcohol services, with relapse-prevention medicines considered as eTG advises;
  • smoking cessation support.

Complications and safety netting

Complications include:

  • peripancreatic fluid collections, necrosis (which may become infected) and pseudocysts;
  • ARDS, AKI and shock;
  • hypocalcaemia and hyperglycaemia;
  • splenic vein thrombosis;
  • recurrent attacks and chronic pancreatitis, with diabetes and malabsorption, if drinking continues.

Nurses escalate a rising HR, falling BP, rising RR or falling SpO2, low urine output, fever, worsening pain, confusion or signs of withdrawal: a clinical review for any yellow-zone value and a rapid response for any red-zone value. After discharge Gary sees his GP within 1 to 2 weeks for alcohol support, his blood pressure, cardiovascular risk and weight. He returns to the ED for returning abdominal pain, vomiting, fever or yellow skin or eyes.
points: Acute pancreatitis needs 2 of 3 criteria: typical epigastric pain through to the back, lipase more than 3 times the upper limit, and characteristic imaging. The height of the lipase does not reflect severity.

Gallstones (about 50%) and alcohol (about 25%) cause most cases. Every patient needs an ultrasound for gallstones plus calcium and triglycerides; an early ALT above about 150 U/L points to gallstones.

Severity (revised Atlanta) depends on organ failure and whether it persists beyond 48 hours. Early warning signs are SIRS, a raised haematocrit, rising urea or creatinine and a CRP above 150 mg/L at 48 hours.

Manage with goal-directed IV fluids (not aggressive large volumes) to a urine output target, titrated opioid analgesia with regular paracetamol, an antiemetic, early oral or enteral feeding, VTE prophylaxis and no prophylactic antibiotics.

In alcohol-related pancreatitis, give parenteral thiamine before glucose, record the time of the last drink, monitor for withdrawal and offer a non-judgemental brief intervention with drug and alcohol referral.
Always exclude the dangerous mimics of epigastric pain through to the back: ruptured AAA, perforated ulcer, inferior MI and, when the pain follows forceful vomiting, Boerhaave syndrome.
